## Setting the LILO Password

With LILO you are vulnerable only to single-user mode or booting into an insecure operating system. LILO can be configured to ask for a password before any operating system or kernel on the system is booted. LILO configuration was discussed in Chapter 6.

To configure the LILO global password add the **password=***<password>*** line, where **password** is the new LILO password. You are not hashing the password, so it is plain text in the file. Figure 12-2 shows the /etc/lilo.conf file.

### FIGURE 12-2
lilo.conf file.

```
boot=/dev/sda
map=/boot/map
default="linux"
keytable=/boot/us.klt
prompt
nowarn
timeout=100
message=/boot/message
menu-scheme=wb:wb:wb:bw
password=myPassWord03
image=/boot/vmlinuz
	label="linux"
	root=/dev/sda1
	initrd=/boot/initrd.img
	append="devfs=mount acpi=off"
	read-only
image=/boot/vmlinuz
	label="failsafe"
	root=/dev/sda1
	initrd=/boot/initrd.img
	append="devfs=nomount acpi=off failsafe"
	other=/dev/fd0
```

Any time you change /etc/lilo.conf you must run the */sbin/lilo* -v command. This line installs the LILO boot loader and will be activated the next time you boot the system.

## Password Security

By default, during installation, the Linux operating system is set to use MD5 and shadow passwords. These offer secure user verification before allowing access to the system.

Even MD5 passwords can eventually be cracked. If an individual gains access to the system, the /etc/passwd file can be copied to another machine and the passwords it contains can be broken with password cracking programs. If strong passwords are not used, the MD5 passwords can be broken in minutes.

The `/etc/shadow` file is used when shadow passwords are enabled. This file is read-only by the root user, so other users cannot get to the `/etc/shadow` password file even if they are logged on the system.

If the password file cannot be copied and cracked on a remote computer, the only way an unauthorized user can break into the system is by using SSH or Telnet and trying passwords. This process is much slower and easily tracked using system logs. However, if the Linux users are using weak passwords, an unauthorized user may break into the system quickly; and even if the breach is detected, it is likely to be after the fact.

## Strong Passwords

It’s amazing how many users have passwords such as god, 1234, a birthday (such as 061064), jsmith, the name of their dog, and other easily guessed values—even the word “password.” These kinds of passwords can be figured out in a few minutes, especially if you know the user. Even without knowledge about the user, cracking software can figure the passwords out in very little time. Some password cracking programs use a dictionary as a database of possible passwords and, in some cases, can send passwords to the host computer until one works.

The best defense against this kind of attack is to use *strong passwords*. A strong password contains letters (uppercase and lowercase), numbers, special characters (!, $, #, etc.), and a minimum length of eight characters. Strong passwords can completely deter unauthorized users.

Passwords should be as long as possible; but as with any good security measure, they have drawbacks. Requiring users to type ten or more characters to log on may cause more confusion than it’s worth. You will find that users forget their passwords; or worse yet, they will write them down and tape them to a drawer, monitor, or keyboard. For that reason, eight characters tends to be enough to deter the occasional unauthorized user while still making it somewhat easier for a user to remember.

The Linux operating system is case sensitive, so mix uppercase and lowercase letters within the password. Using uppercase and lowercase letters increases the number of possible passwords exponentially. Add special characters such as !, $, or # and numbers, and the possibilities increase even more.

Using strong passwords is important to deny access to unauthorized users; but strong passwords will not be used if they are too hard to remember. Some tips for designing passwords as well as remembering them follow.

Start with a mnemonic that you will remember; for example, a song lyric such as “Are you lonesome tonight, do you miss me tonight.” Write down the first letter of each word as a beginning password. Preserve the case of the letters and keep any punctuation within the song lyric:

*Aylt,dy mmt*

Replace certain letters with numbers. For example, replace any letter o with a zero (0), or any letter d with a number six (6), so the password now reads:

*Aylt,6ymmt*

Replace certain letters or numbers with special characters. For example, replace a small letter a with the “at” sign (@), a letter i with an exclamation point, and so on. Now our password looks like:

*Ay!t,6ymmt*

You have the idea. Be consistent with your replacements and you will always remember your password and have a very strong password.

Change passwords often. Even though you use strong passwords, that doesn’t mean they will never be cracked. Recently, a user received an e-mail supposedly from the LAN administrator requesting the user’s password to fix a problem that had been discovered. Of course, the user sent the password. You never know where a compromised password will come from. The maximum amount of time a user should keep a password is 90 days.

Users should not repeat passwords. Some users may have two or three passwords that they rotate. This consistency can lead to easy cracking of passwords.

Never use the same password on several different machines. If one machine is compromised, your account on all the machines may be compromised.

### Testing Passwords

As an administrator, you may want to test the passwords of your users. The best test is to see if you can crack the passwords. There are many password cracking programs that run under Linux, Windows, Unix, and Apple Macintosh. Two common programs are:

- **John the Ripper** This password cracker is available for a number of operating systems. Its purpose is to detect weak Linux passwords. It takes a password or shadow password file as input and returns the usernames and passwords discovered.
- **Crack** This password cracker is one of the oldest and probably the fastest. It is available for Linux systems.

![](img/37f079cee226b270f2e09b37a2e4a05d_334_0.png)

The following is a copy of a shadow password file. Users jsmith, rbrown, and ksmith have passwords equal to their IDs. Users dengle and davidengle both used strong passwords and were not cracked. User myuser was cracked after about ten minutes.

```
dengle:$1$Rafj$SG$Iftf/8Shq$jIsV9kNo5Vc/:12307:0:99999:7:::
jsmith:$1$k1Kp8$Oxg$aRnLX6/Bvy$7t848ho5flU/:12364:0:99999:7:::
myuser:$1$SV3$9bpk.r$f674RsoaH$GmyhWHPC9$8k1:12348:0:99999:7:::
guest::!:12348:0:99999:7:::
davidengle:$1$Px$99kZ$XV$HbSOSuF$739MCD$3XVgh$5k0:12348:0:99999:7:::
rbrown:$1$W$duIYNY$PV$KWHMxz$W/Dcb$YzP.7FWvh.:12364:0:99999:7:::
ksmith:$1$7$hNnA$ThO$R4YgaCArv9R4$j85GY$2HE.:12364:0:99999:7:::
```

The DOS version of John the Ripper was used to crack the passwd file. The file was copied from the server to a file named passwd.txt in a Windows directory.

```
F:\john\JOHN-16\RUN>john passwd.txt
Loaded 6 passwords with 6 different salts (FreeBSD MD5 [32/32])
jsmith   (jsmith)
rbrown   (rbrown)
ksmith   (ksmith)
```

## Administrative Control

Never run a Linux system as root. The root login has full control of the operating system, and an accidental command can have serious consequences. Nevertheless, on any system, there is a need to execute programs with the root user privileges. One way to enable users to execute root commands safely is through a setuid program such as sudo or su. A setuid program operates with the user ID of the owner of the program rather than that of the user operating the program.

### Disable Root Login
You can disable root logins using the /etc/security file. This file lists ttys from which root may log in to the Linux operating system. The /etc/security file is a list of available login devices. To disallow root log in, just remove the entries from the file. Typically, the only login device for the root user is console. An easy way to remove all the entries is with the `echo > /etc/security` command.
